title: Endgame? Middlegame?
reviewNotes: Reviewed full narration and montage: the creator explicitly explains that the follower’s losses occur in the middlegame, then reviews queen blunders, knight forks and planning. There is no endgame study to reconstruct. Keep the searchable source; outside Endgame Stories study scope, not an information gap.
transcript: This is day 10 of reviewing my followers games every single day until I hit 100,000 followers. Today is the turn of Abdallah and if you want to be next, all you have to do is leave a like, follow me, and comment your chess.com username. Abdallah says my end games are bad, but I don't know end games to learn and how to learn them. Well, Abdallah, I have to strongly disagree with you. I had a look at a lot of your games and I really struggled to find any games that ended with an end game. As a matter of fact, almost every position you lose, you lose in the middle game. For example, in this game, there is a total of five blunders that you have played. So, let's have a look at what's going on. You are playing with white, your opening is fine, you develop your pieces, all of this is good, you play a lot of book moves, and it doesn't take too long for your opponent to blunder a piece, which you correctly capture. But now, here is where everything starts to go south. You hang your queen in one move. Queen to F3 loses the queen with a check to the knight. Now, a couple of things are interesting to me in this position because you played this move after about 30 seconds of thoughts, which tells me that you correctly assess the position, thought about a few different options, and eventually decided to play this move, which is a blunder. And that, in my opinion, can only mean two things. You are either thinking about the wrong things and not considering enough what your opponent's pieces are doing, and in this case, this is the only piece close to your position, so it's really the only piece that we need to pay attention to, or this was a case of total tunnel vision, where you were stuck on some kind of idea, and you completely just, for some reason, missed the knight. Somehow, your opponent misses it, so now you move the queen away, hopefully because you now saw that the queen was hanging, and now you play bishop to F4, which the engine doesn't mind, but from a human standpoint, I really don't like this move because after black's next move, you're giving up the bishop pair for pretty much no reason. But what's even worse is that on the next move, you bring the queen back to D2, and this is yet again a blunder. Not only that, it's a blunder for the next few moves because both you and your opponent missed the fact that all this time the knight could have delivered a fork picking up the queen and winning the game. Of course, that cannot be done directly here because the knight is defending that square. But after a move like c5, you're going to lose your knight because if you move it, well, you're going to lose the queen and that's worse. So, this move queen to d2 tells me a bunch of things. Again, you are not paying enough attention to your opponent's ideas and you are getting a little bit lost in terms of how to come up with a plan in this middle game. There is no particular reason why the queen shouldn't stay here. You can focus on moving the rooks to a more active square, bringing the king to a more safe square, starting a pawn attack on this side of the board, improving these pieces. There is a lot of very good free content out there about middle game and how to come up with a plan and how to find your opponent's plans. So, if I were you, I would focus on that for the moment.
